newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin back in Kremlin on Monday.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin back in Kremlin on Monday.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin returns to the Kremlin next Monday, nearly seven weeks after undergoing open heart surgery, but doctors have warned him against taking on too much work and straining his steady recovery.

Yeltsin's press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing on Friday that the 65-year-old president would return to Moscow over the weekend from the Rus country residence outside the capital where he has been convalescing.
"The doctors recommend for a certain time a light regime -- a staged, gentle resumption of work in order not to overload the president," Yastrzhembsky said.
Yeltsin, who has been largely absent from the Kremlin since he was re-elected for a second term in July, underwent a quintuple heart bypass operation on November 5.

His government, battling a prolonged economic downturn, serious wage arrears and poor tax collection, received a boost on Friday when the State Duma lower house of parliament backed the 1997 draft budget on its second reading.
The Duma, though dominated by Yeltsin's communist and nationalist opponents, approved the draft by 248 votes to 114.
The spending plans now have only to clear a third and final reading in the Duma before passing on to the more cooperative upper house Federation Council.

Even if the draft budget becomes law by the end of 1996, Yeltsin still faces a daunting array of problems as he reclaims the helm of his vast country but his successful heart surgery should give him renewed energy for the political fray.

Yastrzhembsky recalled the prediction of pioneering U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey that the president had "at least 10 years of active working life" ahead of him on condition that he did not overdo things. DeBakey was a consultant to Yeltsin.
"We will do our utmost to make his return a smooth process," Yastrzhembsky told reporters.
Yeltsin was expected to appear on television later on Friday. First brief footage showed him in relaxed mood, wearing an open-necked shirt and cardigan.
Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin's plans for his first days back at work included meetings with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais and other senior officials.

Touching on problems in Russia's cash-strapped armed forces and with tax collection, Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin would also attend sessions of the Defence Council and of a special tax commission, but did not say when the meetings would take place.
But Yastrzhembsky denied media reports that Yeltsin intended to mark his return to work with major personnel changes.
"One should not expect that the president's return to work will immediately herald weighty decisions affecting the country's fate," he said.
Yeltsin's long absence from the Kremlin triggered some frenzied jostling for position within his entourage.

Among the most pressing tasks awaiting Yeltsin will be keeping a fragile peace deal on track in breakaway Chechnya, where Russia is pulling out its last troops ahead of planned presidential and parliamentary elections there on January 27.
The peace process came under renewed pressure this week after gunmen shot dead six foreign aid workers in Chechnya.
On Friday the security service of Chechnya's separatist government said it had detained several people suspected of involvement in the murders, Itar-Tass news agency said.
